claims.text: Brittle behavior in compositionally complex high-entropy alloys emerges primarily from processing-induced nanoscale microstructural instabilities rather than grain-boundary segregation or large-scale precipitation.
Processing-induced nanoscale microstructural instabilities act as local stress concentrators.
Selective laser melting may introduce localized dislocation pile-ups or nanoscale inclusions near grain boundaries.
SLM-induced heterogeneities lower hot ductility under high-temperature, rapid-loading conditions.
The initial high-entropy alloy is single phase.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution and minimal conventional grain-boundary precipitates.
Localized nanoscale heterogeneities emerge at or near grain boundaries.
Variations in SLM processing promote microstructural defects.
The SLM-induced defects concentrate stress and facilitate premature crack initiation.
Nanoscale defects reduce the material's ability to dissipate energy.
Reduced energy dissipation produces lower ductility and a brittle failure mode distinct from segregation- or intermetallic-precipitation-driven failure.
SLM-processed HEAs will show significantly lower hot ductility than conventionally processed HEAs under high-temperature, rapid-loading conditions.
SLM-processed HEAs will show a higher incidence of brittle fracture than conventionally processed HEAs under high-temperature, rapid-loading conditions.
Conventionally processed HEAs should retain a more uniform microstructure and higher toughness than SLM-processed HEAs.
The conventionally processed baseline has a uniform, nearly defect-free microstructure and robust toughness under the tested service conditions.
The processing-route effect is most pronounced during high-temperature service and rapid loading.
Differences between SLM and conventional processing routes may be smaller outside high-temperature, rapid-loading regimes.
